title: Bernoulli distribution
summary: A Bernoulli random variable is the indicator of an event. It equals 1 with probability p, and its mean and variance are p and p(1-p).
intuition:
A Bernoulli random variable records a single yes-or-no trial. Code a success as 1 and a failure as 0. If the success probability is p, then $P(X=1)=p$ and $P(X=0)=1-p$. A coin toss, a defective item, and the indicator that a roll is a multiple of 3 are all Bernoulli once you have named the event and its probability. There is no third outcome hiding in the model.

The mean is p. That is not a coincidence of algebra so much as the definition of an indicator: the long-run fraction of trials that land on 1 is the probability of the event. The variance is p(1-p). It is small when the trial is nearly certain to go one way, and it is largest at p=1/2, where it equals 1/4. Because X is 0 or 1, the square X^2 equals X, so the second moment is also p and the variance is p minus p squared.

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=p,\qquad \mathrm{Var}(X)=p(1-p).
$$

A binomial count is a sum of independent Bernoulli trials with the same p. One trial is the whole Bernoulli distribution: Binomial(1, p) is Bernoulli(p). The indicator language is the one to keep, because linearity of expectation applies to indicators even when the events are dependent. The variance formula p(1-p) is for a single trial. Dependent indicators still have that marginal variance, but the variance of their sum picks up covariances.

definitions.body: One experiment with two outcomes. The variable $X$ equals 1 with probability $p$ and equals 0 with probability $1-p$.
The indicator $I_A$ of an event $A$ is the Bernoulli variable with $p=P(A)$. Then $\mathbb{E}[I_A]=P(A)$.
The parameter $p=P(X=1)$, with $0\le p\le 1$. It is the mean of $X$. It is not the variance.

formulas.name: Mass function
formulas.note: There are no other points in the support.

formulas.name: Mean and variance
formulas.note: The variance is at most $1/4$, at $p=1/2$.

formulas.name: Indicator expectation
formulas.note: This is why a count of events has mean equal to the sum of the probabilities, dependence or not.

properties: The mean equals the success probability $p$. The variance equals $p(1-p)$, which is also $\mathbb{E}[X^2]-(\mathbb{E}[X])^2$ with $\mathbb{E}[X^2]=p$.
The variance is maximised at $p=1/2$, where it equals $1/4$. It is 0 at $p=0$ and at $p=1$.
For any constant $a$, $\mathrm{Var}(aX)=a^2 p(1-p)$. Scaling the 0-1 variable by 2 multiplies the variance by 4.
Bernoulli($p$) is the special case Binomial($1,p$). A sum of $n$ i.i.d. copies is Binomial($n,p$) only when the copies are independent.
Two different events can have indicator variables that are dependent. Each indicator is still Bernoulli, with its own $p$.

examples.title: A trial with p = 3/10
examples.prompt: Let $X$ be Bernoulli with $P(X=1)=3/10$. Find the mean and the variance.
steps: The mean of a Bernoulli variable is the success probability, so $\mathbb{E}[X]=3/10$.
The second-moment route agrees: $X^2=X$, so $\mathbb{E}[X^2]=3/10$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)=3/10-(3/10)^2=3/10-9/100=21/100$.
examples.answer: The mean is $3/10$ and the variance is $21/100$.

examples.title: Indicator of a multiple of 3
examples.prompt: A fair die is rolled once. Let $X$ be 1 when the face is a multiple of 3, and 0 otherwise. Find $p$, the mean, and the variance.
steps: The event is $\{3,6\}$, so $p=P(X=1)=2/6=1/3$. Thus $X$ is Bernoulli($1/3$) and the mean is $1/3$.
examples.answer: Here $p=1/3$, the mean is $1/3$, and the variance is $2/9$.

traps: Reporting the variance as $p^2$, or as $p$. The variance is $p(1-p)$. The quantity $p^2$ is $(\mathbb{E}[X])^2$, and $p$ is $\mathbb{E}[X^2]$ as well as the mean.
Forgetting that an indicator is Bernoulli. If $P(A)=p$ then $I_A$ has mean $p$ and variance $p(1-p)$, even when you never write the mass function.
Using $\mathrm{Var}(aX)=a\,\mathrm{Var}(X)$. The constant comes out squared: $\mathrm{Var}(2X)=4p(1-p)$.
Solving $p(1-p)=c$ and keeping the root above $1/2$ when the problem says the success probability is at most $1/2$. The two roots sum to 1.
python:
from fractions import Fraction
p = Fraction(3, 10)
assert p * (1 - p) == Fraction(21, 100)
q = Fraction(1, 3)
assert q * (1 - q) == Fraction(2, 9)
assert Fraction(2, 5) * Fraction(3, 5) == Fraction(6, 25)
assert abs(0.2 * 0.8 - 0.16) < 1e-12
print(float(p * (1 - p)), float(q * (1 - q)))

questions.stem: X is Bernoulli with success probability $2/5$. The variance of X is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $6/25$.

The variance is $p(1-p)=(2/5)(3/5)=6/25$. Option B is the mean. Option C is $p^2$, which is the square of the mean rather than the variance. Option D is $1-p$, the probability of a zero.

questions.stem: The indicator $I_A$ of an event with $P(A)=0.2$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[I_A^2]=$
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $0.2$.

An indicator is 0 or 1, so $I_A^2=I_A$ and the second moment equals the mean, which is $P(A)=0.2$. Option B is $p^2=(\mathbb{E}[I_A])^2$, not $\mathbb{E}[I_A^2]$. Option C is the variance $0.2\times 0.8=0.16$. Option D would be right only for an indicator that is always 1.

questions.stem: X is Bernoulli($p$) with $0<p<1$. Which of the following are true?
options: The variance can be larger than $1/2$.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

The mean and variance formulas are $p$ and $p(1-p)$. Because $X$ is 0 or 1, one of $X$ and $1-X$ is always 0, so the product is 0. The variance $p(1-p)$ has maximum $1/4$ at $p=1/2$, so it cannot exceed $1/2$.

questions.stem: A biased coin has $P(H)=1/4$, and $X$ is the indicator of heads. Which of the following are true?
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

$X$ is Bernoulli($1/4$), so the mean is $1/4$, the failure probability is $3/4$, and the variance is $(1/4)(3/4)=3/16$. The variance of $2X$ is $2^2\times 3/16=3/4$, not $3/16$, so D is false.

questions.stem: X is Bernoulli($p$) with $\mathrm{Var}(X)=0.16$ and $p\le 1/2$. Enter $100p$.
questions.solution:
The answer is **20**.

Solve $p(1-p)=0.16$, or $p^2-p+0.16=0$. The discriminant is $1-0.64=0.36$, so the roots are $(1\pm 0.6)/2$, that is $0.8$ and $0.2$. The condition $p\le 1/2$ selects $p=0.2$, and $100p=20$. Both roots give the same variance because $p$ and $1-p$ trade places.
